prompt: A tiny canary has seen only a few requests and no errors. The regression you care about is rare. What should the release pipeline conclude?

options.text: No errors proves the new version is safe
options.explanation: A small sample may simply never exercise the rare failure.

options.text: Evidence is insufficient; choose enough representative traffic and observation time before expanding
options.explanation: Correct. Limit exposure while collecting enough evidence for the regression and delayed effects being tested.

options.text: Immediately expose all users to make errors easier to see
options.explanation: That abandons the canary’s risk boundary.

options.text: A fixed short bake time guarantees statistical significance at any traffic rate
options.explanation: Evidence depends on volume, variability, effect size and the chosen test, not time alone.

workedExample: Ask whether the canary has exercised the relevant behaviours often enough. More traffic or more time can improve evidence; a representative simultaneous baseline helps distinguish release effects from shared changes. No universal count of observed errors proves safety.

prompt: A global service runs in 20 regions, each made of independent cells. A deploy with a latent bug triggers only under traffic patterns seen in some regions. Which rollout plan best limits blast radius while still finishing in reasonable time?

options.text: Deploy to all 20 regions at once, with automated rollback if errors rise
options.explanation: Automated rollback helps, but all users have received the new version before the rollback triggers; actual impact depends on which traffic activates the bug. Exposure isn't limited at all.

options.text: Blue-green switch of the whole global fleet after testing in staging
options.explanation: Staging didn't reproduce the regional traffic pattern, so the bug passes testing and then hits all users at the switch.

options.text: Waves: one box → one cell → one region → a few regions → the rest, with automated canary analysis and bake time at each stage
options.explanation: Correct. Staged waves (as AWS describes) cap exposure at each step, give region-specific traffic a chance to trigger the bug while impact is small, and roll back automatically on regression. The cost is that full rollout takes hours to days.

options.text: Deploy to the smallest region only and, if fine after an hour, everywhere else
options.explanation: Better than all-at-once, but a single small region may not exhibit the traffic pattern that triggers the bug, and the jump straight from one region to nineteen gives a huge blast radius.

workedExample:
Compare worst-case exposure when the bug triggers:

| Plan | Users exposed |
|---|---|
| All at once | 100% |
| Global blue-green | 100% |
| 1 small region → rest | Almost the entire remaining fleet if missed |
| Waves | cumulative deployed footprint |

Wave design:
1. One box in one cell: catches crashes and obvious errors.
2. One cell: real traffic mix for that cell's customers.
3. One region, then 2–3 diverse regions: different traffic shapes, so the regional bug is likely triggered here, at a limited footprint determined by regional traffic; already-deployed regions also remain exposed.
4. Remaining regions in larger waves.

Automated rollback at each stage, plus bake time long enough to see daily patterns, makes this hands-off.

link.title: Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: A canary receives a small fraction of traffic while the old version handles the rest. Its raw error count is lower. How should you assess whether it improved reliability?

options.text: Compare error rates and relevant latency/business outcomes against a representative simultaneous baseline, with enough evidence
options.explanation: Correct. Different request counts make raw error totals incomparable; also account for cohorts, variation and correlated faults.

options.text: Declare success because the canary has fewer errors in total
options.explanation: It also handles fewer requests, which can explain that difference.

options.text: Compare the canary only with last month’s fleet average
options.explanation: Traffic and external conditions can change; a contemporaneous representative baseline reduces this confounding.

options.text: Assume equal-sized groups remove every source of bias
options.explanation: Equal counts do not guarantee comparable users or independent observations.

workedExample: First establish each group’s exposure and traffic mix. Compare rates or distributions over the same interval, and evaluate uncertainty with a suitable test. A simultaneous baseline helps with shared time effects but cannot fix a biased cohort or hidden correlation. Expand only when the evidence and rollback plan support it.
